intro_html: Traverse to Switzerland's highest pass in the Bernese Alps, passing turquoise Oeschinensee and the historic Blüemlisalphütte hut. Spectacular alpine panorama.

photos.alt: Hohtürli ridge and Blüemlisalp from the hike

routes.title_html: Kandersteg → Oeschinen Lake → Oeschinen Pass → Blüemlisalphüette → Hohtürli Pass (classical T3 traverse)
bullets_html: • Griesalp Trailhead (1,408 m) — Starting point in upper Kiental
• Alpiglen Alp (~1,800 m) — First major grazing meadow with trail junction
• Sefinental Valley (~2,100 m) — Alpine valley with stream crossings; begins steepening
• Alpine Meadows & Moraine (~2,400–2,600 m) — Final push through scree/cairn terrain
• Hohtürli Pass (2,778 m) — Summit col; small cairn between Wildi Frau & Dündenhorn
• Descent Switchbacks (~2,400–2,000 m) — Steep descent on scree toward Kandersteg
• Kandersteg Valley Floor (1,174 m) — Final approach through meadows to village

getting_there.by_pt_html: Train: Bern HB → Frutigen (30 min) → Kandersteg (10 min). Plan via sbb.ch — typically a direct regional train from Bern. Kandersteg is a car-free mountain village with shuttle buses from the main parking area to the trailhead.
getting_there.by_car_html: Drive to Kandersteg via the A6 freeway from Frutigen (Bern direction). Follow regional roads toward the Oeschinen valley. Pay parking is available at the Kandersteg trailhead area near the lake access.

day_plans.title: Day 1
rows: Start at Griesalp trailhead; head toward Alpiglen Alp
Reach Alpiglen Alp (~1,800 m); continue into Sefinental Valley
Begin major elevation gain; cross Sefinental stream (ankle to mid-calf depth)
Reach alpine meadows & moraine (~2,400 m); final climb via cairn markers
Summit Hohtürli Pass (2,778 m); spectacular alpine panorama
Begin descent toward Kandersteg; steep switchbacks on scree terrain
Reach valley meadows; final approach to Kandersteg village
day_plans.footer_html: Total time: 7–9 hours depending on fitness & pauses. Early start (6–7 AM) essential; aim to descend before 3 PM to avoid afternoon thunderstorms.

lapse_rate.example_html: Example: 20 °C at Kandersteg → ~7 °C at Hohtürli summit

weather.season_html: July–September is the main season; the hut is typically open from mid-June to mid-October. Snow can linger into July; avoid after fresh snowfall as the pass terrain becomes serious.

takeaways_html: Weather is the controlling factor: Rapid conditions changes at/above 2,500 m are common. Clear mornings often deteriorate to cloud/rain by afternoon. Trip reports strongly recommend early starts (6–7 AM) and descent before 3 PM.
Sefinental creek crossings are the bottleneck: High-water season (May–early July) can be difficult; many reports note water thigh-deep after rain. Trekking poles are mandatory; water shoes helpful.
Solitude vs. traffic: Alpine Pass Route users pass in clusters; independent day-hikers are sparse. The pass itself is rarely crowded, but Kandersteg & Griesalp bus terminals create bottlenecks.

reports.title: Kandersteg to Hohtürli — Alpine traverse
bullets_html: • Exposed alpine ridge with cairns; wind can be extreme

reports.title: Oeschinen Pass to Blüemlisalphüette hut overnight
bullets_html: • Two-day trip allows rest at historic SAC hut
• Turquoise Oeschinen Lake is photogenic early-morning stop

gear.title: Essential
items_html:
• Hiking poles
  • Sun protection (cream + glasses + hat)
  • 2 L water
  • Emergency snacks

safety_html: Exposure: Rocky ridge sections near the pass with exposed ledges; trail mostly stable but demands careful footing, especially in descent.
Scree Fields: Loose rock dominant on south descent; stable on ascent. Risk of falls from destabilized stones.
Stream Crossings: Sefinental creek crossings (ankle- to mid-calf depth); snowmelt (May–July) raises water levels significantly. Use poles or sticks for support.
Weather Deterioration: Pass at 2,778 m highly exposed to rapid weather changes; afternoon thunderstorms common (Jun–Aug).
Scrambling Sections (T3): Final ascent requires hand-holds on rocky terrain; not technical but exposed and demanding sure-footedness.
Navigation: Occasional poor trail marking above 2,400 m in poor visibility; GPS/map essential in clouds.
Turn back if thunderstorms develop — lightning risk above treeline is extreme.
disclaimer_html: This page is an informal hike plan, not professional mountain-safety advice. Conditions change rapidly. Always check MeteoSwiss and SAC before setting out.
